prompt:
An image is attached as a VISUAL STYLE REFERENCE ONLY: the original LatentWorld method overview. Generate a NEW and DIFFERENT DriveCompose scientific overview using the complete specification below. The attached image is not an edit target and is not DriveCompose evidence. Learn only restrained graphical density, distinct spatial representations and clean typography; keep DriveCompose topology, labels and scientific relationships exactly as specified below.

Create one complete scientific method-overview illustration for DriveCompose, a computer-vision research project about composable Gaussian driving worlds. Use case: scientific-educational. Asset type: a high-quality raster design draft for a two-column CVPR paper overview. All printed labels are English. The explanatory scenes are schematic scientific illustrations, not photographs or purported experimental renderings. Draw an actual visual explanation with recognizable road geometry, vehicle and articulated-human representations, sparse spatial queries, token sequences, attention relationships, decoded Gaussian primitives, and state-controlled reuse. The output must look like a carefully composed computer-vision paper figure with concise labels, readable scientific relationships and clean white space.

SCIENTIFIC MESSAGE AND SCOPE

The figure explains this single message: partial multi-camera driving observations are converted into an observation-anchored, jointly completed Gaussian world; its background and canonical vehicle/human assets are then reused under multiple simulation states. The scientific intervention is joint completion across heterogeneous canonical representations while reliable observations are kept fixed and known free space is suppressed. The main question is how the hidden road surface, a vehicle's unseen side and a person's unseen surface can become usable three-dimensional content without overwriting the surfaces supported by the log.

Show an offline construction pathway followed by a clearly delimited online state-controlled pathway. Offline construction includes shared evidence recovery, canonical query support, typed latent encoding, multi-step conditional flow completion, typed Gaussian decoding and an observed-view check. Online execution reads fixed world content and a current state, assembles transformed Gaussians and renders observations. The state can change through an external policy and dynamics backend. Only that current state changes during online execution; the generated canonical content remains fixed. These scopes must be evident from the picture rather than being dependent on the caption.

The figure is a method illustration. It contains no benchmark scores, plots, claimed quality improvements, quantitative tables or examples presented as real model outputs. Draw the driving scene in a restrained three-dimensional schematic style using ellipsoidal Gaussian marks, planar road geometry and simple recognizable object contours. Small image-like fields are diagrammatic camera views of the same illustrative scene, with consistent car and person identities. They must not imitate captured Waymo photographs or pretend to preserve empirical pixels. No paper venue logo, dataset logo or institutional logo should appear.

VISUAL INFLUENCES AND THEIR LIMITED ROLE

CANVAS, SCALE AND OVERALL COMPOSITION

Use a very wide landscape canvas with an aspect ratio close to 2.2:1, approximately 3300 by 1500 pixels or the closest high-resolution equivalent. The intended final paper width is about 178 mm. Aim for primary labels near an effective 8-point size and secondary labels near 7 points at that width. If the amount of content threatens readability, simplify subordinate labels and retain the concrete scientific relationships. Do not solve crowding by adding tiny text. Keep a clean white background without texture, decorative shadows, gradients, frames resembling software windows or a full-width poster title.

Organize five neighboring scientific regions along a continuous left-to-right reading spine. Their usable horizontal proportions are approximately: 18 percent observations and shared evidence; 19 percent canonical query construction; 36 percent joint completion; 15 percent typed decoding and fixed world; 12 percent state-driven reuse. These are relative explanatory masses, not rigid equal-width cards. The focal joint-completion region must be the first visually distinctive structure. Let its local/global interaction glyph and matched before/after token lanes occupy meaningful area. Keep the left encoder compact and the right application branch secondary.

Reserve a narrow top strip for small panel captions: '(a) Driving observations', '(b) Canonical queries', '(c) Observation-anchored joint completion', '(d) Fixed Gaussian world', '(e) State-driven reuse'. The long central caption can occupy the full width of its focal region; do not force it into the same tiny width as the other captions. Use short medium-weight sans-serif lettering. The caption text is smaller than the main objects but remains readable. No huge 'Overview' banner is necessary. If the word 'DriveCompose' is used, place it quietly next to the first caption rather than giving it its own large band.

REGION A: PARTIAL DRIVING OBSERVATIONS AND SHARED RECOVERY

At the far left, draw a compact stack or staggered pair of small camera-view frames. Each depicts the same simple schematic road scene from a different calibrated camera and time. Include a gray road, a blue partial car silhouette and a blue partial person silhouette. Use a modest depth cue and identical object identity across the frames. Do not render a rich photographic city. A small camera-frustum glyph and a short two-tick time cue below the frames explain multiple cameras and times without a long formula. The main label directly below the stack is 'Multi-camera logs'.

Make the incompleteness visible: the camera-facing portions of the car and person are solid blue, their unseen portions are indicated by a light-gray dashed contour or a gap, and a road patch occluded behind the car is absent or stippled. These markings are schematic visibility cues. The missing rear surface should not look like a physically sliced car; keep the full object outline faintly available while emphasizing that its surface has not been observed. Place no red warning crosses over the whole scene. The visible limitation should be expressed by the missing spatial support, not by a large sentence.

Connect the camera-view stack with one primary arrow to a small flat operator labeled 'Driving Log Encoder'. The encoder can be represented by a compact stack of two or three feature planes entering a simple rectangular operator, but it must remain subordinate to the central completion. A small adjacent label 'Geometry, identity, state' names its output. The input log includes images, calibration and time; recovered state includes the original camera and actor poses. There is no language prompt or future action entering this encoder.

REGION B: HETEROGENEOUS CANONICAL QUERY SUPPORT

Draw three aligned spatial rows: background on top, a rigid vehicle in the middle, and a canonical human below. The background row contains a finite road-and-building patch as a sparse world-coordinate support. Use small blue points on reliably observed road surface and light-gray grid cells in an occluded road patch. The background remains in world coordinates. Add a tiny axis triad next to the road patch with the short label 'World'. The gray grid is reserved query support, not an output occupancy probability map.

The vehicle row shows the observed car in its original world placement and a small arrow that removes its changing root pose, arriving at a centered canonical car with a local axis triad. Label the canonical representation 'Vehicle local'. Show several blue observed surface anchors and a faint regular support grid spanning the fixed local bounding volume. The car's local dimensions and geometry remain fixed across runtime states. Avoid wheels drawn on independent joint axes, suspension arrows, deforming vehicle parts or an articulated vehicle skeleton.

The human row shows a person being placed into a simple canonical pose with a skeletal stick structure and an enclosing partial surface made of points. Label it 'Human canonical'. Use blue points on observed portions and light gray on unobserved surface support. The canonical support and binding weights come from an identity-specific template. A tiny skinning-weight cue can be a few short lines linking surface points to nearby bones, but it should not dominate or imply measured weight values. Keep the human full body recognizable; do not reduce the person to an unlabeled dot.

Include the sky as a small subordinate direction-domain cue associated with the background row: a tiny cube or hemisphere with several direction arrows, labeled 'Sky directions'. It is a fourth token type, not a fourth physical asset standing on the road. Do not give it a vehicle-style metric bounding box. Background coordinates are metric world coordinates; sky coordinates are unit directions. The sky cue can share the background decoder later, but must not be drawn as a movable object. Do not suggest that every unobserved sky direction is validated.

Make the canonical support's observation classification concrete. In a compact three-item legend under these rows, use a filled blue point for 'Observed', a light gray point for 'Unknown', and a hollow hatched cell for 'Free'. The free cell means reliable evidence of empty space. It is distinct from an unobserved cell and should not become an orange surface later. Keep blue points and gray unknown points in matching positions as they transition into latent strips. The legend may be near the lower left of the focal region if that improves fit, but it should explain all subsequent color meanings.

Use compact query-to-token arrows from each spatial row into its corresponding typed latent row. A narrow shared operator at the boundary is labeled 'Typed encoding'. Each type uses its own projection into a common latent width. The illustration can use one operator bracket covering the three rows with separate entry ports, rather than three large duplicate boxes. Do not draw an all-token average that collapses separate assets into a single vector. Multiple vehicles and people are supported conceptually, but show one representative of each for readability.

REGION C: THE FOCAL OBSERVATION-ANCHORED JOINT COMPLETION

This region is the largest and most technically expressive scene. Give it a faint warm off-white background or an almost invisible violet-gray boundary. Inside it, show three horizontal latent-query lanes aligned with the spatial rows: 'Background', 'Vehicle', and 'Human'. Include a small sky-direction token subgroup next to the background lane. Tokens are small rectangular or square cells associated with fixed query locations. They must look like structured representations rather than colorful arbitrary confetti.

On the left side of each lane, show a partial latent strip containing filled blue observed tokens, neutral light-gray unknown tokens and one hollow free-space token where appropriate. On the right side, show a matching completed strip: blue observed tokens remain in the same positions, formerly unknown surface tokens become amber/orange, and free-space cells remain hollow. The correspondence is query identity and support position; do not imply that all latent values for different queries are identical. Use a few matching outline marks to help follow the same support locations without printing invented numbers.

At the center of each row, use one compact light neutral block labeled 'Local attention' or a common aligned header 'Local attention' above the three blocks. Each block receives only its own local group. The background block represents spatial neighborhoods, the vehicle block one canonical asset, and the human block one canonical asset. A small dotted group outline around a subset of tokens makes locality visible. Do not connect every pair of cells with a web of lines; three or four explicit representative dependencies are enough to express grouped interaction.

Above the local blocks, draw a shared horizontal memory bar containing a small sequence of neutral violet-gray slots. Label it 'Global memory'. Draw clean up/down read-and-write arrows between each local row and this shared memory. The incoming read arrows reach the memory bar; the returning write arrows reach the associated local token row or local operation. Keep their arrowheads distinguishable, using separate nearby lanes if necessary. These relationships explain how background, vehicle and human conditions are exchanged within one completion model. Shared enclosure without actual connection arrows is insufficient.

Place one compact two-part condition glyph near the top-left edge of the joint region: two coordinate triads linked to a small token, with the label 'Canonical + world-reference'. The canonical triad attaches conceptually to asset shape identity; the world-reference triad attaches to the asset's reference placement in the background scene. Feed this glyph into the completion mechanism with a short dashed conditioning arrow. It must be clear that reference placement is a condition for offline completion, not a physical collision solver and not an instruction to deform the car when its pose changes.

Below the three lanes, show a compact conditional-flow strip from noise to completed unknown content. Use a left patch of gray noise tokens, a thin rightward integration arrow and a right patch whose unknown entries are amber. Label this strip 'Conditional flow'. Use tau rather than online simulation time for its integration coordinate. If using math, print only a short 'tau: 0 to 1' label; do not invent a denoising-step schedule or a measured iteration count. The default source uses multiple steps, but no particular step count is essential to this overview.

Show a small local loop at the right side of the conditional-flow strip labeled 'Repeat'. Its returning arrow lands on the update state or local completion block. It is an integration loop during offline construction, not a loop through the driving policy and not a branch that regenerates assets once per simulation frame. Keep this loop within region C. Do not let its arc surround the input encoder, fixed world and output rollouts, because that would imply the wrong update scope.

Make the observed-anchor path explicit. A thin blue bypass originates from the observed latent condition on the left, travels along a reserved lower lane inside region C and enters a small projection junction immediately after the flow update. Label the junction 'Clamp observed'. Its visual output contains the same blue observed cells seen before the update. This is overwriting protected entries with their observed codes, not adding two full latent vectors together. Use a simple clamp or lock glyph plus matching blue cells. Do not place a plus sign at this junction.

The free-space condition has its own small hollow-cell glyph and short label 'Suppress free space'. A thin auxiliary edge goes to the per-step projection, and another short continuation reaches the Gaussian opacity gate on the decoding side. This encodes the two actual protections: free latent entries are reset to zero, and non-sky Gaussian opacity for free support is explicitly zero. The hollow cells must not turn into amber filled cells, solid obstacles or opaque road surfaces. Free-space constraints are based on reliable observations; the figure does not claim uncertainty-free ground truth.

REGION D: TYPED GAUSSIAN DECODING AND ONE FIXED WORLD

At the right of the completed latent strips, draw three short type-specific decoding operators, arranged as aligned row endpoints and labeled concisely 'Background', 'Vehicle' and 'Human' under a common heading 'Gaussian decoders'. The background endpoint also has a very small sky-cube cue. These are separate decoding paths with geometry appropriate to their type. They are not three unrelated full systems. A decoder may use a small wedge shape or thin flat box, but keep a consistent shape grammar for all three.

After each decoding operator, draw a compact spatial Gaussian representation made of small ellipses: a world-coordinate road patch for background; a canonical car for vehicle; and a canonical human plus skeleton for the human. Blue ellipses depict observed-supported content and amber ellipses depict completed surface support. Render Gaussian marks as a restrained spatial point/ellipsoid field, without neon particles, explosive clouds or an impression of physical material escaping from objects. The geometry should still read as road, car and person at a glance.

Group the decoded outputs into a single compact composable-world representation. Use a small isometric road tile with a background point field plus adjacent canonical asset silhouettes or an understated asset-library bracket. A quiet lock glyph or the word 'Fixed' communicates immutability after offline construction. Print 'Fixed Gaussian world' as its main label. Show exactly one persistent world, not a new generated world for each output camera. The canonical assets remain associated with their stable identity even though their runtime placements differ.

Include a small observed-view checking scene before accepting the fixed world. This can be a compact diamond or two overlapping camera-plane outlines labeled 'Observed-view check'. It receives the decoded candidate path and a thin local reference path labeled 'Observed-only'. The observed-only representation is decoded through the same fixed codec from the protected observed code; it is a comparison reference, not a second independently trained decoder. A tiny local original-view frame next to the check supplies the original observation reference. Keep the visual scene small but sufficiently explicit that fixed-code preservation and rendering-level occlusion checking are different operations.

REGION E: STATE-DRIVEN REUSE AND THE APPLICATION BOUNDARY

To the right of the fixed world, draw a compact operation labeled 'Compose & render'. Give it two visibly distinct inputs: one solid arrow carrying the fixed world, and one state arrow from a small state glyph. The state glyph includes a camera frustum, a car heading arrow and a small skeletal pose cue. Its main label is 'Current state'. It does not feed into the completion DiT. It supplies root poses, active asset identities and human articulation to the renderer/composer.

Show two or three small vertically arranged schematic output scenes connected by a short branching line from the same fixed world and state-driven operation. One can be labeled 'New view', one 'Vehicle pose' and one 'Human pose'. These are explanatory state interventions, not time steps with measured timestamps. Maintain the same road tile, the same car identity and the same person identity. Change the camera in the first, the car's whole-body pose in the second, and the person's skeletal pose in the third. Blue/amber surface ownership remains stable across the examples.

For the vehicle intervention, draw the complete car rotated or translated rigidly, including its wheels moving with the body. Do not flex its dimensions or add independent wheel-spin arrows. For the human intervention, draw the fixed canonical surface following a bent elbow, shifted leg or walking pose through its skeleton and root pose. The person's identity and canonical clothing volume remain fixed. The illustration must make this distinction recognizable through the pose glyphs, not through a dense paragraph.

Under the state-driven operation, include a small bounded return loop labeled 'External policy / dynamics'. An arrow from the observation side goes to this external backend, and its update arrow returns only to 'Current state'. The feedback path must stay in the rightmost region. Use a slightly lighter outline or a dashed external-module boundary. Do not connect the external backend back to the encoder, canonical queries, joint-completion memory or the fixed-world content. This distinction is essential to understanding what the method learns.

SEMANTIC PALETTE AND SHAPE GRAMMAR

Use a small consistent palette with dark blue-gray ink around #253447 on white. Reliable observed surface/tokens use a restrained medium blue close to #4B86B4 with a pale blue fill where appropriate. Newly completed surface/tokens use amber close to #E8A35B. Unknown support is light gray around #D7DCE2. Free-space support is white/hollow with gray diagonal hatching. Use a muted violet-gray only for attention/memory operators and a very faint warm neutral tint behind the central mechanism. Do not assign a different bright color to every asset class or module.

Blue and amber encode observation provenance, not asset category. Therefore the vehicle and human both contain blue observed and amber completed parts. Their category is conveyed by recognizable geometry, separate rows and short labels. Global memory is neutral violet-gray because it is an operator/learned state rather than observed surface. The same color meaning must hold in input fields, spatial queries, latent strips, decoded Gaussians and output interventions. No unexplained red/green success/failure coding should compete with this palette.

Keep line behavior precise. Main data arrows are solid dark blue-gray with consistent arrowheads and moderate weight. Conditions are thinner dashed lines; observed clamping can use a blue thin line; explanatory associations use fine dotted lines without implying a tensor flow. Real branch and merge points can have tiny junction dots; accidental crossings must not. Reserve enough end clearance that arrowheads touch object boundaries cleanly and do not cover the car, skeleton, token cells or text. Use a small number of orthogonal turns or gentle curves, not tangled routes.

TYPOGRAPHY, LABEL BUDGET AND CONTENT PRIORITIES

Use a clean paper-oriented sans-serif family similar to Arial, Helvetica or a neutral scientific sans. Main section captions use medium weight, operator names use regular or semibold, and tiny coordinate labels remain regular. Maintain only a few functional sizes. All printed words must be spelled correctly and have enough background clearance. Prefer one or two short lines per operator. The center title may be larger than subordinate labels, but not so large that it replaces the mechanism itself.

The essential visible labels are: 'Multi-camera logs'; 'Driving Log Encoder'; 'Geometry, identity, state'; 'Canonical queries'; 'World'; 'Vehicle local'; 'Human canonical'; 'Sky directions'; 'Typed encoding'; 'Joint Completion DiT'; 'Local attention'; 'Global memory'; 'Scene context'; 'Canonical + world-reference'; 'Conditional flow'; 'Clamp observed'; 'Suppress free space'; 'Gaussian decoders'; 'Observed-view check'; 'Observed-only'; 'Original views'; 'Fixed Gaussian world'; 'Current state'; 'Compose & render'; 'Same world, multiple states'; 'External policy / dynamics'. The small legend uses 'Observed', 'Unknown', 'Free', and 'Completed'. Asset-row labels and the optional output-case labels should be short and placed next to the objects they identify.

SCIENTIFIC INVARIANTS AND WHAT CHANGES VISIBLY

FINAL COMPOSITION AND QUALITY EXPECTATIONS

Render the complete DriveCompose method illustration with this scientific topology and these visual roles. Preserve all essential conditioning and update boundaries. The finished image contains concise scientific labels and schematic scenes only, with no template slots, production instructions, reference credits or reviewer notes printed in the image. The visual draft is intended for user review before any editable reconstruction; the artwork itself should be confident, readable and aesthetically appropriate for a modern CVPR method overview.
